Business
bĭz'nĕs
n. (that which occupies a man; his employment or affair — in Scripture both the Father's business and the honest labour of one's own hands)
From busy (Anglo-Saxon bysig) plus -ness: literally the state of being busy, hence the thing that occupies. The commercial narrowing of the word is modern; in 1611 it meant any occupation or matter in hand.

Biblical Definition

Business in the Authorized Version means whatever a man has in hand, and Scripture speaks well of it. The Lord Jesus uses it of His own vocation at twelve years old, in His first recorded words: “wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?” (Luk 2:49). Paul places diligence in daily work inside a list of spiritual duties without any sense of descending a level: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord” (Rom 12:11) — the three clauses belong together, and a man cannot claim the second while neglecting the first. To the Thessalonians, some of whom had stopped working in expectation of the Lord's return, he writes: “study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you” (1Th 4:11). And Proverbs promises that competence is noticed: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men” (Pro 22:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines business as employment; that which occupies the time and attention; and also as an affair, a matter in hand, or a concern of any kind.

expand to see more

BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time, attention and labor of men, for the purpose of profit or improvement.

2. Any particular occupation or employment engaged in for a livelihood or gain, as agriculture, trade or a profession.

3. Affair; concern; that which engages the attention.

You have undertaken a business that is above your reach.

4. Serious engagement; important occupation, in distinction from trivial affairs.

Key Scripture

Luk 2:49 — "And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

Rom 12:11 — "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;"

1Th 4:11 — "And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;"

Pro 22:29 — "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men."

Modern Corruption

A sacred-secular divide is imposed on Scripture, so that ministry counts as the Lord's work and ordinary labour does not — and, on the other side, business is baptised as a ministry to excuse whatever it takes to succeed.

expand to see more

Rom 12:11 does not permit the divide. Paul writes not slothful in business, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord as one breath, and Col 3:23 makes it explicit for the lowest station in the ancient world: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” — addressed to slaves. The Reformation recovered this against the medieval assumption that the monastic life was the higher calling; Luther's doctrine of vocation and Calvin's treatment of the ordinary station both rest on it. A carpenter, a nurse, and a pastor are all in the Lord's work, and only one of them draws a salary from the church.

The corollary corruption is the entrepreneurial gospel that treats a company as a ministry in order to sanctify its ambitions, so that ruthlessness becomes stewardship and self-promotion becomes influence. 1Th 4:11 sets a strikingly unglamorous standard: study to be quiet, do your own business, work with your own hands. Paul's stated reason follows in the next verse — that ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing. Ordinary competent work, done quietly, is a testimony, and it is the one Scripture actually commands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English busy + -ness; rendering Greek spoude (G4710), diligence, in Rom 12:11, and ta tou patros, “the things of my Father”, in Luk 2:49, and Hebrew melakah (H4399), work or occupation.

expand to see more

Hebrew melakah (H4399) — work, occupation, business; the word for the labour forbidden on the sabbath and for a craftsman's trade.

Greek spoude (G4710) — haste, earnestness, diligence; “not slothful in business” is literally not lagging in diligence.

Greek ta tou patros mou — “the things of my Father” (Luk 2:49); the KJV supplies business, others house; both senses are in the phrase.

Greek ta idia — “your own business” (1Th 4:11); the same construction Paul uses against the busybodies of 2Th 3:11.

Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to be a busybody, literally to work around a thing; the counterfeit of real business.

Usage

"“About my Father's business” — the Lord's first recorded words, at twelve."

"“Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit” — one breath, not two categories."

"“Diligent in his business… shall stand before kings” — competence is noticed."
